messages.content: Can you get the weather data for Antwerpen by sending a request to the weather API URL? Use latitude 51.2194 and longitude 4.4025, and I'd like the response in JSON format.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.reasoning:
The user wants us to fetch weather data for Antwerp using the weather API URL. We need to use the function calls. The function is named requests_get. We'll call it with url set to the weather API URL. But we don't know what the weather API URL is. Possibly it's something like "https://api.weather.com/v1/geocode/{lat}/{lon}/forecast.json"? Or maybe "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast". The user didn't specify the exact endpoint. We might need to guess or ask clarifying question. But the instruction says "Use latitude 51.2194 and longitude 4.4025, and I'd like the response in JSON format." So we need to call the function with those params.

We need to decide on a weather API. The user said "weather API URL". That could refer to some known public API. Maybe open-meteo.com. Let's assume open-meteo. The typical request: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=51.2194&longitude=4.4025&current_weather=true. That returns JSON. So we can call that.

Thus we call requests_get with url "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast", params {lat: 51.2194, lon: 4.4025, current_weather: true}. But the function signature expects params keys: lat, lon, format. There's no current_weather param. But we can include it anyway; the function doesn't restrict unknown keys. But the function signature only lists lat, lon, format. So we can't pass current_weather. But we can pass format: "json". But the API expects "format=json" maybe. Actually open-meteo uses "format=json" as default. So we can just pass lat, lon, and maybe "current_weather": true. But the function signature doesn't allow arbitrary keys. But we can still pass them; the function may ignore unknown keys. But let's keep it simple: pass lat, lon, format: "json".

But open-meteo requires "current_weather=true" to return current weather. Without it, it returns forecast. But we can still get forecast. The user didn't specify what kind of data. They just want weather data. So we can provide forecast.

Alternatively, we can use "https://api.met.no/weatherapi/locationforecast/2.0/compact?lat=51.2194&lon=4.4025". That returns XML by default. But we can set "Accept: application/json". But the function signature has Accept header. We can set Accept: "application/json". And format param maybe "json". But the function signature includes format param. So we can set format: "json". That might produce JSON.

Let's choose open-meteo because it's simpler. So we call:

requests_get({
  url: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
  params: {
    lat: 51.2194,
    lon: 4.4025,
    current_weather: true,
    temperature_unit: "celsius",
    windspeed_unit: "km/h",
    timezone: "Europe/Brussels"
  },
  headers: {
    Accept: "application/json"
  }
})

But the function signature only allows lat, lon, format. But we can pass other keys. The function might accept them. But the signature is limited. However, the function description says "Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request." It lists lat, lon, format. But we can add others. It's okay.

So we call the function with the above.
